scope.end: 38b: Rav Yosef's ruling on an egg roasted by an urn and Mar son of Ravina's proof, which continues on 39a

sections.title: The Forgotten Pot: Eating Food That Cooked on Shabbat, and the Decree
sections.gist: May one eat from a pot left on the stove that cooked on Shabbat? The section covers two readings of R. Chiyya bar Abba's ruling, a baraita of R. Meir and R. Yehuda, Rav's account of the decree, and R. Yosei's shriveled eggs in Tzippori.

children.title: 'Ve'lo Shena': Is Forgetting More Lenient Than Cooking, or Stricter?
children.gist: R. Chiyya bar Abba compares the forgotten pot to cooking on Shabbat. Rabba and Rav Yosef read him leniently, Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak stringently.

bullets.text: A dilemma is put to R. Chiyya bar Abba. One forgot a pot on the stove before Shabbat and it cooked on Shabbat: may the food be eaten? He was silent.
The next day he taught publicly: one who cooks on Shabbat unwittingly may eat it, and one who cooks intentionally may not, "and the halakha is no different" (*ve'lo shena*).
Rabba and Rav Yosef read this leniently. A cook performs an act, so if he acted intentionally he may not eat. One who forgot a pot performs no act, so he may eat even if he left it intentionally.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak reads it stringently. No one will cook deliberately and then feign innocence, so an unwitting cook may eat. But one who leaves a pot could leave it on purpose and say "I forgot". So the Sages penalized him, and he may not eat even when he truly forgot.

chart.caption: Two readings of R. Chiyya bar Abba's *ve'lo shena*
columns: How the forgotten pot compares to cooking
rows: Leaving a pot is not an act; cooking is
He might leave it on purpose and claim he forgot, so the Sages penalized him

children.title: The Baraita: R. Meir Permits Fully Cooked Food, R. Yehuda Only What Deteriorates
children.gist: Food not fully cooked depends on whether it was forgotten or left on purpose. For food already fully cooked, R. Meir permits everything, while R. Yehuda splits water, which deteriorates, from food, which improves.

bullets.text: Baraita: one forgot a pot on the stove and it cooked on Shabbat. If he did so unwittingly he may eat it; if intentionally, he may not.

That applies to water not fully heated and food not fully cooked. If the water was fully heated or the food fully cooked, he may eat whether he left it unwittingly or intentionally. That is R. Meir's view.
R. Yehuda: fully heated water is permitted, since it evaporates and gets worse (*mitztamek ve'ra lo*). He won't come to stoke the coals.
Fully cooked food is forbidden, since it shrivels and improves (*mitztamek ve'yafeh lo*), and he may stoke the coals.
The general rule: whatever shrivels and improves (cabbage, beans, meat cut in small pieces) is forbidden. Whatever shrivels and deteriorates is permitted.

chart.caption: The baraita's case of fully heated water and fully cooked food, and how the Gemara reconciles each tanna with his view elsewhere (38a.7)
rows: May be eaten, unwitting or intentional
May be eaten, unwitting or intentional
Here he speaks after the fact; elsewhere he forbids *shehiyah* ab initio
Forbidden: it shrivels and improves (cabbage, beans, small pieces of meat)
Here the stove is not *garuf ve'katum*; elsewhere it is

children.title: The Baraita Against Both Readings: Before the Decree, or Kashya
children.gist: The baraita permits food forgotten unwittingly. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak dates it before the decree, but for Rabba and Rav Yosef it remains a difficulty.

bullets.text: The baraita permits food not fully cooked that was left on the stove unwittingly.
For Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak this is no problem. The baraita was taught before the decree against deceit, and his ruling applies after it.

For Rabba and Rav Yosef, neither dating works. If the baraita was taught before the decree, its ban on intentional leaving contradicts them, since they permit that. If it was taught after the decree, its ruling on unwitting leaving doesn't fit their view either.
No answer is found. *Kashya*: the objection stands.

returns_to.note: Tests the two readings of *ve'lo shena* against the baraita

children.title: Rav's Account of the Decree: Why Even the One Who Forgot Was Penalized
children.gist: At first a forgotten pot was treated like unwitting cooking. When people began leaving pots on purpose and claiming they forgot, the Sages penalized even the one who forgot.

bullets.text: The decree is reported by Rav Yehuda bar Shmuel, from R. Abba, from Rav Kahana, from Rav.
At first they said: one who cooks on Shabbat unwittingly may eat, and intentionally may not. The same held for one who forgot a pot on the stove and it cooked on Shabbat.
When many began leaving pots intentionally and saying "we forgot", the Sages imposed a *kenas*: even the one who forgot may not eat.

children.title: R. Meir and R. Yehuda Against Themselves: Ab Initio or After, Swept or Not
children.gist: Each tanna seems to contradict his view on the chapter's first baraita. R. Meir is resolved as ab initio vs. after the fact, and R. Yehuda as a swept vs. an unswept stove.

bullets.text: In the baraita at the start of the chapter, R. Meir says even Beit Hillel forbid *shehiyah*, and R. Yehuda says Beit Hillel permit it. Here R. Meir is lenient and R. Yehuda strict.
R. Meir: there he forbids leaving food ab initio; here he permits eating it after the fact, even if it was left intentionally.
R. Yehuda: there he permits a stove that is *garuf ve'katum*; here he forbids one that is not.

returns_to.note: Returns to the R. Meir–R. Yehuda baraita to reconcile it with the chapter's opening baraita

children.title: One Who Left a Pot on Purpose: R. Yosei in Tzippori and the Shriveled Eggs
children.gist: Is one who deliberately left his pot penalized? The proof from R. Yosei in Tzippori is deflected, but it shows that shriveled eggs improve, as Rav Chama bar Chanina's meal with Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi confirms.

bullets.text: Dilemma: one who transgressed and left his pot on the stove. Did the Sages penalize him, forbidding the food, or not?

Shmuel bar Natan citing R. Chanina: in Tzippori, R. Yosei found hot water left on the stove and did not forbid it. He found shriveled eggs left there and forbade them. Presumably he forbade eating them that Shabbat.
Rejected: he only forbade leaving them ab initio on a following Shabbat, not eating them that Shabbat. The proof falls, and the dilemma gets no answer here.
The distinction implies that shriveled eggs are *mitztamek ve'yafeh lo*. The Gemara confirms it: yes.
Rav Chama bar Chanina: he and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi were guests together and were served eggs shriveled to the size of crab apples (*uzradin*), and they ate many of them.

sections.title: Chazarah on Shabbat: 'Even Return', Hand or Ground, and Intention
sections.gist: Beit Hillel's "even return" applies on Shabbat itself. The discussion then asks whether a pot set on the ground may be returned, how intention to return matters, and three unresolved in-between cases.

chart.caption: Returning a pot to the stove on Shabbat: where it was set down, and what he intended. (Rav Dimi and Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda, both citing R. Elazar, split between the first two views without the text saying which holds which.)
columns: In hand, meant to return it
On the ground, meant to return it
On the ground, didn't mean to

children.title: 'Even Return' Means Even on Shabbat: Rav Sheshet and Rav Oshaya's Kettle
children.gist: Beit Hillel permit *chazarah* on Shabbat itself, and Rav Oshaya proves it from R. Chiyya the Great's silence.

bullets.text: The Mishnah: Beit Hillel say one may even return a pot to the stove. Rav Sheshet: on that view, even on Shabbat itself, not only on Shabbat eve.

Rav Oshaya agrees. On Shabbat they passed a kettle (*kumkemos*) of hot water up to R. Chiyya the Great from the lower floor (*deyota*), poured him a cup and put the kettle back on the stove, and he said nothing.

illustration.caption: Rav Oshaya's account (38a–38b): on Shabbat the kettle was brought up to R. Chiyya the Great, a cup was poured, and the kettle was put back on the stove below. His silence shows that *chazarah* is permitted even on Shabbat.

children.title: Set on the Ground: R. Tadai Forbids, R. Yochanan Permits
children.gist: R. Tadai allows returning a pot only while it is still in hand. R. Ami rejects his view as a private one and cites R. Yochanan permitting it even from the ground.

bullets.text: R. Zerika, from R. Abba, from R. Tadai: returning is allowed only while the pot is still in his hand. Once he sets it on the ground, he has shown he changed his mind about the fire, and returning is forbidden.
R. Ami: R. Tadai acted and spoke on his own. R. Chiyya citing R. Yochanan: even if he set it on the ground, he may return it.

children.title: Rav Dimi vs. Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda, and Abaye's Two Versions on Intention
children.gist: The hand-or-ground dispute recurs in R. Elazar's name. Abaye then adds the question of whether he meant to return the pot, in two versions that differ on which factor controls.

bullets.text: Rav Dimi and Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda disagree, both citing R. Elazar. One permits returning only from the hand; the other permits it even from the ground.
Chizkiya citing Abaye, first version: even in hand it is permitted only if he meant from the start to return it. So from the ground it is forbidden even if he meant to.
Second version: from the ground it is forbidden only if he didn't mean to return it. So in hand it is permitted even without that intention.

children.title: Neither Hand nor Ground: A Stick, a Bed, Another Urn — Teiku
children.gist: Cases between holding the pot and putting it down are raised and left unresolved.

bullets.text: R. Yirmeya: what if he hung the pot on a stick, or set it on a bed?
Rav Ashi: what if he moved it from one urn to another?
*Teiku*: the questions stand.

sections.title: Oven and Kupach: Heat Beyond the Kirah's
sections.gist: The Mishnah forbids the oven and makes the kupach depend on its fuel. The Gemara then asks about leaning a pot against them, why the kupach is intermediate, and what a kupach is.

children.title: Mishnah: The Oven Never; the Kupach Depends on Its Fuel
children.gist: An oven is forbidden even with light fuel. A kupach is like a *kirah* with straw or rakings, and like an oven with pomace or wood.

bullets.text: An oven lit even with straw or rakings: on Shabbat one may place a pot neither inside it nor on top of it.
A *kupach* lit with straw or rakings is like a *kirah*. Lit with pomace or wood, it is like an oven.

children.title: Leaning a Pot Against an Oven: Rav Yosef, Abaye and Rav Adda bar Ahava
children.gist: Rav Yosef permits leaning a pot against an oven. Abaye objects from the *kupach* clause, Rav Adda bar Ahava deflects by making the case a swept stove, and a baraita supports Abaye.

bullets.text: Rav Yosef: "inside" and "on top" mean exactly that. Leaning a pot against an oven is permitted.

Abaye objects from the *kupach* clause. "Like an oven, forbidden" implies that "like a *kirah*" would be permitted. That can't mean on top of an unswept stove, which is forbidden anyway. So the clause must be about leaning, and leaning against an oven is forbidden.
Rav Adda bar Ahava: the Mishnah deals with a *kupach* and an oven that are *garuf ve'katum*. "Like an oven" means that even swept, a pot may not be placed on top, whereas on a swept *kirah* it may.
A baraita supports Abaye. An oven lit with straw or rakings: no leaning a pot against it, and surely not on top or inside, and surely not if lit with pomace or wood.
The baraita continues: a *kupach* lit with straw or rakings may have a pot leaned against it, but not placed on top. Lit with pomace or wood, not even leaned.

chart.caption: The baraita supporting Abaye: what one may do with a pot by each apparatus

children.title: Why the Kupach Sits in Between: Hotter Than a Kirah, Cooler Than an Oven
children.gist: The fuel changes the ruling for a *kupach* because its heat lies between that of a *kirah* and that of an oven.

bullets.text: Rav Acha son of Rava to Rav Ashi: if a *kupach* is like a *kirah*, even pomace or wood should be permitted; if like an oven, even straw or rakings should be forbidden.
Rav Ashi: its heat is greater than a *kirah*'s and less than an oven's, so its status is intermediate.

children.title: What Is a Kupach? One Pot-Hole, and the Purity Mishnah
children.gist: A *kupach* holds one pot and a *kirah* two. A Mishnah on impurity shows it: a *kirah* split between its holes becomes two stoves, while a split *kupach* is simply broken.

bullets.text: R. Yosei bar Chanina: a *kupach* has one hole, with room for a single pot. A *kirah* is like a double *kupach*, with room for two.
Abaye (some say R. Yirmeya): a Mishnah on impurity teaches this. A *kirah* split lengthwise is pure, a broken vessel. Split widthwise, it remains impure, since it is now two small stoves.
A *kupach* split either way is pure: no room is left for even one pot.

sections.title: Heat Without Fire: An Egg by the Urn, Cloths and Sand, Tiberias' Pipe
sections.gist: The Mishnah forbids roasting an egg by indirect heat and rules on Tiberias' pipe. The Gemara opens with whether a roasted egg incurs a *chatat*.
sections.continues: Continues on 39a: Mar son of Ravina's proof from the Mishnah on salted fish rinsed in hot water, then R. Yosei and the Rabbis on heating with sun-heated objects.

children.title: Mishnah: An Egg by an Urn, in Cloths or in Sand; R. Yosei Permits Cloths
children.gist: Three ways of roasting an egg without fire are forbidden, and R. Yosei dissents only on the cloths.

bullets.text: One may not put a raw egg beside an urn of hot water so that it roasts slightly.
Nor may one wrap it in cloths heated in the sun. R. Yosei permits this.
Nor may one bury it in sun-heated sand or road dust so that it roasts.

children.title: Tiberias' Cold-Water Pipe: Shabbat vs. Yom Tov, Bathing vs. Drinking
children.gist: Water warmed by the hot spring on Shabbat is treated as heated on Shabbat. On Yom Tov it is still forbidden for bathing but permitted for drinking.

bullets.text: The people of Tiberias ran a pipe (*silon*) of cold water through a channel of hot-spring water.
The Sages: if it passed through on Shabbat, it is like hot water heated on Shabbat, forbidden both for bathing and for drinking.
If it passed through on Yom Tov, it is forbidden for bathing but permitted for drinking.

children.title: An Egg Roasted by the Urn After the Fact: Rav Yosef Says Chatat
children.gist: One who went ahead and roasted an egg beside an urn has cooked, says Rav Yosef, and Mar son of Ravina begins a proof from a Mishnah.

bullets.text: Dilemma: what of one who violated the Mishnah and roasted an egg slightly beside an urn?
Rav Yosef: he is liable to a *chatat*, since he performed the Torah labor of cooking.
Mar son of Ravina: we learned something similar in a Mishnah.

children.continues: Continues on 39a: the Mishnah on old salted fish, for which rinsing in hot water completes the cooking, and likewise a slightly roasted egg.

key_terms.sense: leaving food on a heat source into Shabbat
key_terms.definition: Leaving a pot on a fire or stove from before Shabbat so that it stays there on Shabbat. The Sages restricted it for fear one might stoke the coals.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The daf asks whether food left in violation, or merely forgotten, may be eaten, and how Rav's decree penalized even the one who forgot.

key_terms.sense: returning a pot to the heat on Shabbat
key_terms.definition: Putting a pot of cooked food back on a stove on Shabbat after it was taken off. It is more restricted than leaving a pot where it stands.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Beit Hillel's permit applies on Shabbat itself, and the amora'im debate whether setting the pot on the ground, or lacking intention to return it, forbids putting it back.

key_terms.sense: food that improves as it shrivels on the fire
key_terms.definition: Cooked food that gets better the longer it stays on the fire (as opposed to food that is *mitztamek ve'ra lo*, which gets worse). Where food improves, there is concern that one will stoke the coals.
key_terms.on_this_daf: R. Yehuda forbids fully cooked food that improves but permits water that deteriorates, and shriveled eggs are shown to improve.

key_terms.sense: a stove swept of coals or covered with ash
key_terms.definition: A stove whose coals have been swept out or banked under ash. Its reduced heat removes the concern of stoking, so it permits leaving and returning pots on Shabbat.
key_terms.on_this_daf: It reconciles R. Yehuda's two statements, and Rav Adda bar Ahava uses it to read the Mishnah's *kupach* and oven.

key_terms.sense: rabbinic penalty forbidding the product of a violation
key_terms.definition: A penalty imposed by the Sages, often forbidding the benefit of an act, to deter misuse of a lenient rule.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Because people left pots on purpose and claimed they forgot, the Sages penalized even the one who truly forgot, and the Gemara asks whether one who left a pot deliberately is penalized.

judgment_calls: The dilemma about one who left a pot deliberately (R. Yosei in Tzippori and the eggs) is kept inside the forgotten-pot section rather than made its own top-level section, since it asks the same question of eating food left on the stove. The egg story is folded into that section rather than made a lone child.

The baraita's challenge to the two readings (s4) and the self-contradictions of R. Meir and R. Yehuda (s6) are kept in Gemara order as sibling sections with returns_to links, rather than nested under the sections they revisit.

In the chazarah section, R. Yirmeya's and Rav Ashi's unresolved cases (s12) are a separate small section rather than bullets in Abaye's versions, because they open new cases between hand and ground. s11 and s12 share line 38b.4, where the text runs them together.
The two Mishnayot of 38b.10–11 (the egg and Tiberias) and the Gemara on the egg are grouped under one parent on heat without fire, rather than treating Tiberias as a separate top-level section.
The returning chart sits on the parent section (s8) because it compares views from s10 and s11 together.
coverage_notes: No shiur for this daf; the whole outline is built from the Gemara text.
The previous daf's essay ends with Rav Nachman's classification of foods (37b.8) and does not cover the dilemma put to R. Chiyya bar Abba at 37b.9, so the outline starts there.
Sefaria's bracketed explanation at 38a.7 calls the source of 38a.3 a 'Tosefta', while 38a.3 itself introduces it as a baraita. The outline calls it a baraita.
The words 'heated in the sun' for the cloths and the sand in the Mishnah (38b.10) come from Sefaria's interpolated translation and are followed as given.
The Gemara on the roasted egg (38b.12) continues onto 39a; only the start is outlined here, with 'continues' filled in.
